content: In children who consumed non-iron-fortified follow-on formula, the incidence of certain outcomes was 2%, while in those who consumed iron-fortified follow-on formula, it was 6%. No statistically significant differences were observed between these two groups in terms of age, sex, birth length, birth weight, or any other baseline characteristics analyzed in the studies. Van der Gaag (2015) conducted a comparative study examining the effects of dietary advice on full-fat milk and dairy products versus lower-fat milk and dairy products. The authors hypothesized that respiratory tract complaints would decrease in the full-fat group due to the presence of vitamins A, E, and C, which possess antioxidant properties. This was assessed in a retrospective case-control study. The prospective cohort study by Brusner (1993) reported on the incidence of diarrhea and bowel movements in children consuming fortified milk compared to those consuming animal milk. Children receiving fortified milk had fewer episodes of diarrhea and improved stool consistency compared to those consuming animal milk. Baseline characteristics were balanced between the groups. Data indicated that feeding children aged 12–23 months with follow-on formula had similar effects on growth, as measured by body weight and height, compared to animal milk when consumed during 4–12 months of age at a daily intake of 300 mL or more. This effect was consistent regardless of whether the children were breastfed initially or received breast milk substitutes and complementary feeding during their first year of life. The anemia status of the children or the funding source of the study did not influence these outcomes. Feeding children aged 12–23 months with follow-on formula improved their nutrient status, as evidenced by higher vitamin D and iron serum concentrations. These children were also less likely to develop iron deficiency anemia compared to those consuming animal milk. The positive effect on vitamin D was observed when follow-on formula was consumed during 5–12 months of age at a daily intake of more than 150 mL. For a positive effect on iron status, a daily intake of 400 mL was required. Children aged 12–23 months who consumed follow-on formula had higher hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations compared to those consuming animal milk when given 150 mL per day for at least four months. Results from the cross-sectional study by Ghisolfi (2012) supported these findings, showing that follow-on formula reduced the risk of nutrient insufficiency, except for protein intake, where animal milk was more effective. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 44 non-randomized controlled studies (e.g., Chatchatee 2014 and Gill 1997) showed no differences in weight or height outcomes between groups. Information on lower-fat and plant-based milks was limited and primarily focused on nutrient status assessed by lipid serum profiles. Feeding children aged 12–23 months with lower-fat milk did not affect serum lipid profiles, and the response was similar to that observed with full-fat or animal milk. The prospective case-control study by Van der Gaag (2015) demonstrated that children consuming full-fat milk and dairy products for two months experienced a significant reduction in respiratory tract complaints compared to those consuming lower-fat milk and dairy products. Data also suggested that children aged 12–23 months consuming fortified milk, whether full-fat or lower-fat, had similar growth and nutrient status as measured by iron serum concentrations. Children aged 12–23 months consuming fortified milk had higher serum zinc concentrations when given 400 mL per day for six months. They were also more likely to be caries-free compared to those consuming animal milk when given 150 mL on weekdays. Fortified milk reduced the likelihood of anemia and iron deficiency anemia compared to animal milk when consumed at 400 mL per day. However, data on most outcomes were scarce. The quality of evidence was mixed, limiting confidence in the effect estimates. The true effects may differ substantially from the reported estimates. The Brusner (1993) study provided the first evidence of fortified milk reducing gastrointestinal symptoms, such as diarrhea and bowel movements, and improving stool consistency. However, limitations such as unbalanced groups due to the absence of random allocation restricted the interpretation of the findings. No data were available on long-term food preferences, feeding practices, dietary diversity, allergies, or phytoestrogen-related outcomes. The review included 19 studies, of which 16 were RCTs, involving 5,579 children aged 12–23 months. Half of the studies were conducted in high-income countries with low prevalence of anemia, stunting, and wasting, while the other half were conducted in middle-income countries with varied malnutrition prevalence. Studies reporting on anemia and related outcomes, including iron deficiency anemia (IDA), hemoglobin, and ferritin serum concentrations, were conducted in both highand middle-income countries. Growth outcomes were primarily assessed in high-income countries with low undernutrition prevalence. Nutrient composition of animal milk, follow-on formula, and fortified milk varied across studies. The included RCTs were conducted in diverse settings, such as urban and peri-urban areas, daycare centers, and child health centers. Most RCTs from middle-income countries were developed within the context of social programs. These factors are important determinants of malnutrition and overall outcomes. The evidence suggested that feeding children aged 12–23 months with follow-on formula or fortified milk daily improved nutrient status, as assessed by serum concentrations of vitamin D, iron, and zinc. These interventions were more effective than animal milk in various settings. A daily intake of 2 mg of iron per 100 mL for five months was sufficient to improve iron deficiency in high-income countries. However, similar effects were not observed in social programs targeting vulnerable populations. Feeding children aged 12–23 months with follow-on formula had similar effects on iron deficiency anemia as animal milk. However, fortified milk may be effective in reducing anemia and iron deficiency anemia. The effect of follow-on formula on anemia remains uncertain due to a lack of studies reporting on this outcome. Children consuming fortified milk were more likely to be caries-free compared to those consuming animal milk. Fortified milk had similar effects as animal milk on the decayed, missing, and filled surfaces (dmfs) index for molars and canines. Only one study compared the effects of animal milk or no milk on stool frequency, stool weight, fluid, and energy intake, but it did not provide extractable data for analysis. Information on the benefits of plant-based and lower-fat milks was scarce, and no data were available on the effects of animal milk versus no milk in children aged 12–23 months. One study (Svahn 1999) reported on nutrient status measured by lipid serum concentrations in children fed plant-based and lower-fat milks, finding no differences compared to animal milk. No other studies reported data on these outcomes. Only one study compared the effects of follow-on formula versus animal milk on child development index scores (Bayley Mental Development Index and Psychomotor Development Index) and found no effect. The quality of evidence was assessed as low for some studies due to methodological limitations, such as lack of randomization, blinding, and allocation concealment. Some studies had small sample sizes, leading to imprecision in the results. Variability in intervention effects among participants was observed for continuous outcomes, with wide confidence intervals around effect estimates. Methodological inconsistencies, such as differences in blinding and allocation concealment, may have influenced the observed intervention effects. The evidence summarized in the review addressed many key questions but did not adequately address several primary and secondary outcomes. The review process involved independent assessments by two authors, with mutual discussion resolving discrepancies. However, many studies reported outcomes in non-extractable formats, limiting their inclusion in meta-analyses. The review did not impose language restrictions and included extensive searches of grey literature and trial registries. Despite these efforts, the evidence base remains limited for certain outcomes, and the findings should be interpreted with caution.
